answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether advertising a photo of mould is allowed. They also don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach of the minimum standards. Here is what they do cover, as at 1 October 2025.

**Versions applied:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Both metadata records show an end date of 24 November 2025, so both were in force on 1 October 2025.

---

### What the law says

- **The standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising photos:** The provider may enter to produce advertising images and video after giving notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A renter can object in writing to images that show identifying or valuable possessions, and the provider must not take images the renter has objected to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved do not say whether photos showing a defect are permitted.
- **Disclosure to applicants:** The regulations require the provider to disclose to a rental applicant whether the premises comply with the minimum standards, and whether they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp (from 31 December 2021) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is a disclosure duty, not an advertising ban.

### Is the photo enough to prove a breach?

The documents don't set an evidence standard or say how a breach is proven. They also don't say whether a photo is enough. Two points from the text may matter:
- The standard covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), so a photo showing mould doesn't by itself show the cause.
- The photo is taken for advertising, not at move-in, so it doesn't show the condition on the day the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the renter can do or ask

- **Before signing:** Ask the provider in writing whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and whether there has been a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Ask for the condition in the room, since the mould rule applies to each room [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **If the premises don't comply on or just after move-in:** The renter may make a written urgent repair request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure is listed as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified, and the renter may arrange them if the provider doesn't. The renter may be reimbursed up to $2500, and may apply to VCAT if the cost is more than $2500 or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Before moving in:** A renter who has not taken possession may end the agreement on the ground that the premises do not meet any rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable. The renter may apply to VCAT if repairs aren't done within 14 days of the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how a renter would prove the mould's cause, or what a VCAT evidence threshold would be. Those questions would need VCAT decisions or Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance, which weren't in the results.

answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, a notice to vacate stays in effect until it is formally withdrawn. The buyer pulling out does not withdraw it by itself. You may still have grounds to challenge the notice, so get advice before you move out or ignore it.

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, which was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 and so applies on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Sale ground:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(1)).
- **Timing:** The notice must give at least 60 days from when it is given to the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(4)). If the sale contract has conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract has no such conditions, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(2)–(3)).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing and signed by the person who gave the notice and by the renter it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ).
- **Form:** The notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and be accompanied by documentary evidence approved by the Director that supports the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZO).

### What you can do

1. **Check the notice.** Look at when it was given, the termination date (at least 60 days later), whether it was given within the 14-day window relative to the sale contract, whether it is in the prescribed form, and whether the documentary evidence was attached. If something is wrong, the notice may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge it at VCAT.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity, on or before the hearing of any possession application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZS(1)–(2)).
3. **Ask for written withdrawal.** If the landlord withdraws, the withdrawal must be signed by both the landlord and you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ(2)). Don't assume the landlord has withdrawn until you have a signed notice of withdrawal.
4. **Watch for re-letting.** If the landlord obtains possession on this ground, they must not let the premises for use primarily as a residence within 6 months after the notice was given. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person and 750 for a body corporate, unless an exception applies or VCAT determines the premises may be let [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZH).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether a sale-based notice lapses when the sale falls through. The retrieved documents don't say.
- Whether the landlord's stated intention to sell still matters if they no longer sell.
- The date your notice was given, which you'll need to check the 14-day and 30-day deadlines. You didn't provide it.

Because the 30-day challenge window may already be running, contact a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria promptly.

answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set a number of circuits for a rental. They do require a safety standard for circuits that starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after your date. Before then, you can use the electrical safety check and repair rules, which already apply.

**What the law says on 1 March 2023**

- **Circuit rule (not yet in force):** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022) say that "On and from 29 March 2023... all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) meeting a listed AS/NZS standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The rule covers outlets and lighting circuits. It does not say how many circuits there must be, and I found no requirement that heaters or kettles have their own circuit.
- **Electrical safety check (in force now):** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you move in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance duty (in force now):** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," whether or not you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Heater (relevant to your heater):** From 29 March 2023, a fixed heater in good working order must be installed in the main living area of the premises, in a Class 1 building [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Your heater may fall under this, but the documents don't say whether your heater is the "fixed heater" in question.

**What you can ask for or do**

1. **Report in writing now.** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment they supplied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Describe the tripping breaker and when it happens.
2. **Ask for the electrical safety records.** On request, the provider must tell you the date of the most recent electrical safety check, in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can also request a copy of the most recent check, which must be provided within 7 days of the written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The check record must include the electrician's name and licence number, and any repairs required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for a repair in a reasonable time.** The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs "in a reasonable time." If they haven't done so within 14 days of receiving your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can also ask the Director to investigate a breach of the duty to keep premises in good repair, if you have given written notice and the provider hasn't repaired within 14 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs.** Urgent repairs include failure of an essential service or appliance for heating or cooking [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you can't get the provider to act immediately, you may arrange urgent repairs and seek reimbursement for reasonable costs. Reimbursement must be paid within 7 days of your written notice with the cost, and the cap is $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Whether a tripping breaker counts as urgent isn't clear from these documents, so ask the provider and check the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance they point to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Safety defects should also be reported to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Check the 2-year safety check.** If you have no record of a check in the last 2 years, ask the provider to arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The required number of circuits or how the existing wiring must be split.
- Whether an overloaded circuit counts as an urgent repair.
- Any specific rule on kettles or heaters sharing a circuit.

A licensed electrician can tell you whether the circuits meet the standard that starts on 29 March 2023. Note that the Regulations text I retrieved reflects amendments only up to 1 June 2022, so later changes may not be captured.

answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, an agent's email saying the rent is going up is probably not enough. The law requires a formal notice, and a rent increase made without one is invalid. Your agent may still send a valid notice later, so you should check any notice you receive.

Today is 1 October 2025, so the applicable versions are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Required content.** The notice must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **One increase per notice, once every 12 months.** A notice may provide for only one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed terms.** During a fixed term, rent can only increase if the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Check whether you received a valid notice.** The prescribed form is Form 5, which states that the notice must be given at least 60 days before the increase and must include the method used to calculate it. The form also says the rental provider's name cannot be the agent's name [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Director.** If you receive a valid notice and think the proposed rent is excessive, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT.** After the Director's report, you may apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it. You can also apply directly to VCAT, with leave, if you have reasonable grounds for not requesting a report first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Pay the increase during a challenge.** Form 5 states that you will need to pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Effective date:** The documents don't say what date a rent increase takes effect if no valid notice was given. The only start date in the documents is the one stated on a valid notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Whether an email counts:** The documents don't say whether an agent's email could ever satisfy the notice requirement. They do say the notice must be in the prescribed form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Your specific agreement:** I don't have your tenancy agreement, so I can't check whether it has a fixed term or a built-in increase clause.

For help, Form 5 directs renters to the renting section of the Consumer Affairs Victoria website (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) or 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved text does not contain a general rule that makes a notice to vacate void because it followed a repair request. It does give you a 30-day window to challenge a notice at the Tribunal, and it sets out formal requirements the notice must meet.

**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019), which covers 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Formal validity:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the provider or their agent, and specifies the reasons and the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For some grounds it must also be accompanied by supporting documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice:** A renter who receives a notice to vacate under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC may apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, that period would end around 1 December 2019. Please confirm the exact count.
- **Retaliation-related protections in the text:** The only "no effect" provisions I found that refer to exercising a renter's rights are for:
  - a threats-and-intimidation notice (s 91ZK), which is of no effect if given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf); and
  - an end-of-fixed-term notice (s 91ZZD), which is of no effect if given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act or making a report under s 72AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  
  Neither covers a notice based on repairs, and s 91ZZI(1) applies only to fixed-term agreements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because you are month to month, those fixed-term rules probably don't apply to you.
- **Discrimination:** A notice under the repair/renovation-type sections is of no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Your repair rights

- The renter must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Check whether your repair request was in writing.
- If non-urgent repairs are not carried out within 14 days of written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate . The Tribunal can also be asked to order repairs .

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice is **not withdrawn merely because the landlord has not acted on the sale**. Under section 91ZZQ, it is withdrawn only by a written notice signed by both the person who gave it and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to leave merely because the landlord demands it outside the legal process. If you remain after the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the order is reasonable and proportionate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The landlord cannot personally use force to remove you; forcible eviction requires a VCAT possession order and warrant carried out by Victoria Police. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, using a written notice of withdrawal signed by both sides. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to VCAT under section 91ZZS to challenge its validity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies for a possession order, attend the VCAT hearing and explain that the buyer withdrew and ask VCAT to determine whether the notice was valid and whether possession would be reasonable and proportionate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the law said on 1 March 2023

There was **no prescribed rule in the retrieved documents stating how many electrical circuits a rental must have**. The electrical rental minimum standard in force at that date required—**from 29 March 2023**—all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device. That requirement was therefore **not yet in force on 1 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider nevertheless had to keep the premises **in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, and any repair work had to be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The provider also had to arrange an electrical safety check of the electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided **every two years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. You could request the date of the most recent check in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The provider had to give you a copy of the most recent electrical-safety-check record within **7 days** of receiving a written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

**Documents and versions:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 101**, incorporating amendments as at **7 September 2022**; and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at **1 June 2022**. These were the versions in force on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

Write to the rental provider or agent, explain that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater are used together, and request:

1. **An inspection and repair by a licensed or registered electrician**, including checking whether the circuit, outlets, breaker and wiring are safe and adequate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
2. **The date of the most recent electrical safety check**, in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **A copy of the most recent electrical-safety-check record**, which must be provided within 7 days of your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Do not attempt electrical work or interfere with the breaker or any residual-current device yourself; the Act prohibits a renter from removing, deactivating or otherwise interfering with prescribed safety devices unless reasonable in the circumstances, and a residual-current device is a prescribed safety device. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

If the issue is treated as a **non-urgent repair**, you must notify the provider in writing; if it is not repaired within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director to investigate or apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do **not** establish that a breaker tripping under this particular load is automatically an “urgent repair.” Until it is inspected, avoid running the kettle and heater together.

  1. intended to repair, renovate or reconstruct;
  2. had obtained all necessary permits and consents;

  4. gave at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

### 1. Can you fix the damage without telling the owner?
**No.** You have a strict legal obligation to report the damage immediately. 
* **Duty to Notify:** Under section 62 of the Act, as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage, you must give written notice to your residential rental provider (the owner) stating both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If you attempt to fix it secretly without notifying them, you are breaching your duty to report the damage. When you eventually move out, the owner will likely discover the repair during a final inspection, at which point they can still hold you fully financially responsible for the work and potentially charge you for any substandard repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Yes, your rooming house operator is allowed to charge you to use the washing machines. **The Law (as of 15 October 2026)**
*   **Requirement to Provide Laundry Facilities:** Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (v002, in force from 1 December 2024), operators must provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Right to Charge for Services:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115, in force from 13 October 2026) permits rooming house operators to charge residents for services. If they do, they must give you a separate schedule of the service charges before you move in, and provide an itemised account showing your individual use if you use those services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Coin-operated machines are a common method that inherently satisfies the requirement to track individual use.
*   **Breakdowns are Urgent Repairs:** If a washing machine breaks down, it is considered an urgent repair (specifically, the breakdown of an appliance provided for laundering) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The operator must fix it immediately or reimburse you for reasonable costs if you arrange the repair yourself (up to a prescribed limit) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What You Can Do**
1.  **Check Your Documentation:** Ensure you received the required schedule of services before you moved in and that you are receiving itemised accounts for your laundry usage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2.  **Report Breakdowns Immediately:** If a machine breaks, notify the operator immediately as an urgent repair so they can fix it or reimburse you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
3.  **Apply to VCAT if Necessary:** If the operator fails to maintain the machines in good repair, refuses to provide itemised accounts for charges, or enforces unreasonable house rules regarding laundry use, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders to fix the issue [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: Section 109A of the Act specifically allows Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies to impose service charges for laundry if individual usage cannot be accurately measured, but this specific provision only applies to those government/registered providers rather than private rooming house operators. - A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

You may also apply to VCAT for an order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

Both laws below were in force on 1 October 2025. The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). ### What the law says

- **Written notice is required.** A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must include specific details.** It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Only one increase per notice.** A notice may only provide for one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No more than one increase every 12 months.** The rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases.** A rent increase made in contravention of these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed form.** The notice must use Form 5, which states that a valid notice is required for all rent increases [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Who must give it.** On Form 5, the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name," although the agent's address may be used for service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to pay, and from when?

- **Not unless a valid notice was given.** An informal email or a verbal "no" to your negotiation is not a notice in the prescribed form. Based on the documents, an increase without a valid notice would be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing if a valid notice is served.** The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 requires you to pay the increased amount from the start date on the notice, unless VCAT decides otherwise, if you apply to VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So the earliest date would be the start date stated on a valid notice, and that date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given.
- **Documents don't cover the rest.** The documents don't say when an increase would take effect if no valid notice was ever given, whether the agent's email could count as notice, or how the 12-month rule applies to your tenancy, since I don't know your last increase date. They also don't cover back-rent claims.

### What you can do

1. **Ask for the formal notice in writing.** Check that it is on Form 5, is from the rental provider (not the agent), states the amount, the calculation method, and the start date, and was given at least 60 days before that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply for an investigation if you get a valid notice.** You can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given, if you think the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 gives the address GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001, the email renting@justice.vic.gov.au, and the phone number 1300 558 181 for Consumer Affairs Victoria [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** After the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the report. You can also apply directly to VCAT with leave if there are reasonable grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The version in force on 1 November 2019 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 088), which applies from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

Section 91ZZD (end of a fixed term) has a similar bar, but it applies only to fixed-term agreements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I found no general retaliation rule for periodic agreements in the retrieved text.
- **Discrimination is a separate bar.** A notice under sections 91ZX to 91ZZE is of no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Form requirements apply to every notice to vacate under the Division.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the provider or their agent, specify the reason(s), and specify the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Some grounds also require documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging a notice is time-limited.** For notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC, a renter may apply to the Tribunal within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not say whether a notice under other sections has the same window.
- **Reporting repairs.** A renter must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures . Note that this text is from a document that is part of the version above, and the retrieved excerpt says it was inserted by the amendment that is part of version 088 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What to check

1. **The ground on the notice.** Is it a reason listed in the Act, or does it give no reason? A notice that states no valid ground, or that is under a section you don't think applies, may be open to challenge.
2. **Whether the notice meets the form rules.** Is it in writing, signed, addressed to you, and does it state a reason and a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)?
3. **Your repair-request paperwork.** Did you report the leaks in writing as soon as practicable ?
4. **The timing.** If you want to challenge the notice under the 30-day rule, the window runs from when it was given. If it was given on 1 November 2019, 30 days ends on 1 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Confirm this applies to the section your notice relies on.
5. **Your repair rights.** If you arranged urgent repairs and the provider has not reimbursed you within 7 days of written notice, you may apply to the Tribunal under section 209AAB . For non-urgent repairs, you may apply to the Director (section 74) or the Tribunal (section 75) if the provider does not carry out the repairs within 14 days of written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask the provider in writing** which section they rely on and for the reasons, and keep a copy.
- **Apply to the Tribunal** challenging the notice's validity if it falls under a section listed in the 30-day rule, within 30 days of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

Therefore, on the facts given, you do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed that the rent would increase or refused to negotiate. You continue paying the existing rent. ## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088 (in force 2 July 2019–3 December 2019)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- The residential rental provider had to keep the premises in good repair. A renter also had to give written notice as soon as practicable about damage or a breakdown of a provider-supplied fixture. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- If the notice says you must leave so repairs or renovations can be carried out, check whether it relies on **section 91ZX**. That ground required the provider to intend to do the work, hold all necessary permits and consents, and show that the work could not properly be done while you remained. The notice had to give at least **60 days’ notice** and include supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A notice under **section 91ZZO** was invalid unless it was in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, stated the reason, and specified the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- The Act expressly stated that a notice under **section 91ZK** had no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. Section 91ZK concerned alleged serious threats or intimidation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do **not** state a general rule making every notice to vacate invalid merely because it followed a repair request.

## What you can check or ask

1. **Read the stated ground carefully.** Check whether the notice claims repairs under section 91ZX, alleges threats or intimidation under section 91ZK, or gives another reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
2. **Check the timing and paperwork.** A same-day notice would not meet the **60-day** minimum if it relies on the repairs ground. Also check that it is prescribed, signed, addressed to you, gives the reason and termination date, and includes the required evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
3. **Keep evidence of retaliation.** Save your repair requests, photographs, repair reports, emails or texts, the notice, and any messages showing that the notice followed your request. The Act required written reporting of damage or breakdowns, so retain proof of that written notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
4. **Pursue the repair remedy separately.** For non-urgent repairs, after written notice and **14 days** without repair, a renter could apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs; the Tribunal had to hear that application within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For urgent repairs, the Act listed matters including a malfunctioning water-using fixture that wastes a substantial amount of water. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
5. **Ask the Tribunal to consider validity if the notice is pursued.** The retrieved documents specifically provide a challenge process within **30 days** for notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB and 91ZZC. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) They do not state in the retrieved text a separate general application procedure for challenging a retaliatory periodic notice.

- Advertising the property at one rent and then relisting it at a higher rent may be relevant to the prohibition on **false or misleading representations about rent**, but that provision applies only where the provider or agent was **not acting in trade or commerce**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You can ask the provider or agent, in writing, to explain:

1. why they recorded that you withdrew;
2. when and how they say you withdrew;
3. why the advertised rent changed; and
4. whether they or anyone acting for them invited or solicited a higher offer.

Based on the Victorian *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force on 1 October 2025, **no, you do not have to leave** based on that notice if the buyer has pulled out. 

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. The Notice Remains "On Paper" Until Formally Withdrawn
Under Victorian law, a notice to vacate is only formally withdrawn if a specific **notice of withdrawal** is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This document must be in writing and signed by both you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because your landlord has not provided this, the notice technically remains active on paper. 

### 2. The Reason for the Notice No Longer Exists
Your landlord issued this notice specifically because the property was being sold (section 91ZZB) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the buyer has pulled out and the property is no longer being sold with vacant possession, that specific legal ground for the notice has failed. 

### 3. The Landlord Cannot Enforce It
Because the reason for the notice (the sale) is no longer valid, your landlord cannot rely on it to evict you or obtain a possession order from VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If they try to apply to VCAT using this notice, you can challenge its validity because the ground for issuing it is no longer established [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT will not make an order if the notice has been withdrawn or if the reason for it is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What You Should Do
* **Stay in the property:** You are not legally required to vacate based on a notice where the stated reason has fallen through. 
* **Wait for a new notice (if applicable):** If your landlord still intends to sell the property, they must issue a **new** notice to vacate once they have a new contract or firm intention to sell [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Challenge at VCAT if necessary:** If your landlord attempts to take you to VCAT for a possession order, attend the hearing and explain that the sale has fallen through. You can argue that the ground for the notice is no longer valid and that VCAT should dismiss the application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Document Reference:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 110, in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 1 March 2023, here is how your situation is addressed:

### What the law says about electrical circuits
* **No minimum circuit count:** The legislation does not specify a required number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
* **Duty to maintain:** Your rental provider has a strict legal duty to ensure the premises are provided and maintained in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
* **Mandatory safety checks:** The provider must ensure all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings they provide are checked by a licensed or registered electrician every 2 years. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
* **Upcoming circuit breaker & RCD mandate:** Just over a month after your current date (on 29 March 2023), new rental minimum standards come into force requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises to be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker and a Residual Current Device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

### What you can ask for or do
1. **Request Repairs:** Notify your rental provider in writing about the tripping breaker. Because the law requires them to maintain the property in good repair, they must address this issue. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) 
   * If the tripping causes a complete failure of an essential service (like heating or cooking) that cannot be temporarily resolved, it may be classified as an **urgent repair**, which the provider must carry out immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
   * If it is considered non-urgent, they are legally required to complete the repairs within a reasonable time. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask for Safety Check Records:** You can request in writing the date of the most recent electrical safety check and any outstanding recommendations from that report. The provider must supply this within 7 days of your request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **Reference the Upcoming Mandate:** When discussing the issue with your provider, you can note that under the new rental minimum standards taking effect on 29 March 2023, all circuits will be required to have proper circuit breakers and RCDs installed, which may help prevent overloading issues like the one you are experiencing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

*Note: If you choose to reset the breaker yourself, ensure it is safe to do so. If it trips immediately upon resetting, stop using it and contact a licensed electrician or your rental provider.*

**No.** Because you never received an official notice, the agent's email does not legally trigger a rent increase. You do not have to pay the higher amount.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 088 (in force on 1 November 2019), here is what you should check if you believe your notice to vacate is retaliatory:

### 🔍 What You Should Check

**1. Whether the Notice is Legally "of No Effect" Due to Retaliation**
Under Victorian tenancy law, a landlord cannot evict you simply for asking for repairs or exercising your legal rights. The Act explicitly states that a notice to vacate given on certain grounds **is of no effect if it was given in response to**:
* Your exercise (or proposed exercise) of a right under the Act or your tenancy agreement; or
* You making a report about a breach [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
**Check:** Gather dated records of your repair requests, emails, texts, and any responses from the landlord. If you can demonstrate that the notice was issued immediately after you followed up on repairs, this establishes the causal link needed to prove retaliation.

**2. The Stated Reason on the Notice**
A valid notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, specify the exact reason(s) for giving it, and state a valid termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
**Check:** Read the reason listed on your notice carefully. Landlords often use "non-payment of rent" or "successive breaches" as a cover for retaliation. Verify that the stated reason is factually accurate and procedurally correct:
* **If the reason is non-payment of rent:** You must owe at least 14 days' rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). On the first four occasions of non-payment, if you pay the full amount owed by the termination date listed in the notice, the notice automatically becomes of no effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **If the reason is successive breaches:** The landlord can only issue this without a prior warning if you have breached the *same* provision on 2 previous occasions and were given breach of duty notices each time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If they did give you a breach of duty notice for this instance, they cannot issue the eviction until that notice period has passed without compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Whether Required Documentation Was Provided**
If the landlord claims the eviction is due to property repairs, renovations, or demolition, they must have obtained all necessary permits and consents, and the work must genuinely require you to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). They must also provide documentary evidence supporting their reason if required by the notice type [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**4. Your Right to Challenge the Notice**
You are entitled to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the validity of the notice if you believe it is retaliatory, invalid, or procedurally flawed. 
**Check:** Ensure you lodge your application within the strict time limits set by the Act (typically before a possession order hearing or within 60 days for certain notices) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Do not wait until the termination date to act.

### 📝 Summary of Next Steps
1. **Do not ignore the notice.** Treat it as active until a Tribunal orders otherwise.
2. **Document everything.** Compile a timeline showing your repair requests and the immediate issuance of the notice.
3. **Apply to VCAT.** File an application to challenge the validity of the notice, citing that it was given in response to you exercising your right to request repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Pay rent on time.** Ensure no legitimate grounds (like unpaid rent) are left open for the landlord to use against you.

*Note: This information is based strictly on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, as in force on 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For personalised legal advice, contact your local tenancy advocacy service or a community legal centre.*

### What the Law Says
**1. The 14-Day "Deemed Consent" Rule**  
Under section 71C(2) of the Act, a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) is automatically taken to have consented to your pet request if they do not apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While an owner's allergies might be a factor they consider, they cannot simply say "no" and rely on it after the 14-day deadline has passed without involving the Tribunal. A buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw the notice under these provisions.
- **Possession:** The Tribunal (VCAT) can make a possession order only if it is satisfied the notice "has not been withdrawn" and that the renter is still in possession after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It must also find that a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Form requirements:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and, for sale notices, is accompanied by the approved documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

2. **Challenge it if it's defective.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity on or before the hearing of any possession application. Check whether this suits your situation before using it.

**What the law says on 1 March 2023**

- **Electrical safety standard:** Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version 002) requires that "all power outlets and lighting circuits" be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and a switchboard-type residual current device [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The clause does not specify how many circuits a rental must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version 101) requires the provider to ensure rented premises are "provided and maintained" in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Any repairs must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the prescribed minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The standard tenancy agreement form requires the provider to ensure an electrical safety check every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and to provide the date of the most recent check in writing on the renter's request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for**

1. **A written request for the date of the latest electrical safety check.** The provider must provide it on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A copy of the most recent electrical safety check.** This must be provided "within 7 days after receipt by a residential rental provider of a written request from the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **A repair by a suitably qualified person.** Repairs must be done by one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Non-urgent repairs require written notice "as soon as practicable," and the provider must carry them out "in a reasonable time." You may apply to VCAT if the repairs are not done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Compliance with the circuit standard from 29 March 2023.** From that date, the circuit breaker and residual current device requirements apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). - The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have, and I found nothing that makes the single-circuit layout unlawful as of 1 March 2023.

## What the law says

- An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord must not unreasonably withhold consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and must not demand a fee for giving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord may give you a notice to vacate if you have assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent. The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reasons, and specifies a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' Form 6 is the prescribed notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If you don't leave, the landlord must first give a proper notice to vacate before applying to VCAT for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT decides whether it is reasonable and proportionate to make the order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It must consider factors such as whether the breach is trivial and whether it has been remedied as far as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved excerpts don't define "sub-let," so they don't tell me whether a friend simply living with you counts as sub-letting. The documents also don't say how a renter removes a non-party occupant, or how long that takes.

## What you can do or ask

1. **If you want the friend to stay:** Ask the agent or landlord for written consent. They can't unreasonably refuse it or charge a fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they refuse and you believe the refusal is unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

The applicable documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 115 (title: rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 009 (title: rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- **Damage duty:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to rented premises, but damage does not include fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the provider written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Owner's remedies:** The owner may give a repair notice if damage results from the renter's failure to take care. The notice must be in writing and state the damage, and the owner may require repairs within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter does not repair it in a proper and tradesman-like manner within 14 days, the owner may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Can you fix it quickly without telling the owner?**

No, based on these documents. Written notice is required as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so you should notify the owner before any repair. The self-help option is narrow. A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to have the owner do them immediately and the owner is unable or fails to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list which repairs count as urgent. The definition in section 3(1) isn't in the material I retrieved, so I can't confirm whether skirting boards would qualify. For non-urgent repairs, the renter must notify the owner and can apply to VCAT or the Director only if the owner hasn't acted within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any repair must also be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Would it affect the owner's insurance?**

The documents don't say how this damage would affect the owner's insurance policy. The only related point is that a term making the renter liable by default for an insurance excess under the provider's policy is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do now**

1. **Notify the owner in writing** describing the damage, and attach dated photos. Writing is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the owner in writing** to repair it, or to agree in writing that a suitably qualified person can do the work. Keep a record of any reply.
3. **Check your condition report.** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises as far as practicable in the condition they were in when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date, and must give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Photograph the skirting boards** before and after any repair, and keep receipts.

- If an operator charges for services, it must first give the resident a separate schedule of the amount for those services before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must give an itemised account of that individual use [1, s 109].
- Charges for electricity, gas and water are limited to rooms that are separately metered, and the charge must not be more than the supplier's charge. This section doesn't mention laundry [1, s 108].

- **Misleading conduct to induce an agreement:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including false or misleading representations about the rent payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** A provider must not refuse to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you lost out because of discrimination, s 210AA lets you apply to VCAT for compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

A photograph may be relevant evidence: the prescribed condition-report form says photographs may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the premises. ### What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (in force from 6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, **“to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The fact that a buyer has pulled out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only by a **written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, unless the notice is invalid, withdrawn in that way, or set aside by VCAT, you should not assume that you can stay merely because the buyer withdrew. If the landlord applies for a possession order, VCAT must consider whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice and whether it has been withdrawn. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord to give you a **written notice of withdrawal**, signed by both sides. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If you believe the sale reason is no longer genuine or the notice was otherwise invalid, you may apply to VCAT to challenge it **within 30 days after it was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check that the notice was in the prescribed form, stated the sale reason and termination date, and included supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The relevant prescribed form is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### What the law says — 1 March 2023

The documents do **not** state a required number of power circuits for a rental, so they do not establish that your rental must have more than one circuit. **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002**, in force on 1 March 2023, requires the electrical minimum standard only **from 29 March 2023**: all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual-current devices. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure that an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is conducted every **2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician. On request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, with repairs carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

### What you can ask for

Write to the rental provider or agent and report that the breaker trips whenever the kettle and heater run together. Ask them to:

1. arrange a **licensed electrician** to investigate the circuit and make any necessary safety repairs; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)  
2. provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and  
3. provide a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record, which must include the electrician’s details, date, results, required repairs and the report prepared under AS/NZS 3019. That copy must be provided within **7 days** after a written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

You may ask for additional or separate circuits as a proposed remedy, but the retrieved documents do **not** say that you are legally entitled to a particular number of circuits or specifically to a circuit upgrade. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

If the issue is not fixed within a reasonable time, give written notice that repairs are required. If the rental provider has not carried out non-urgent repairs within **14 days** after receiving that notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate or to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that a breaker tripping in these circumstances is automatically an “urgent repair”; urgent repairs expressly include failure or breakdown of an essential service or an appliance provided for heating, cooking or other listed purposes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

**Applicable documents:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 002** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf); *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 101** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
