## What the law says

On 1 October 2025, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (in force from 6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) It requires the rental provider to give **at least 60 days’ notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed form is **Form 5** under the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The form states that a valid notice is required for **all** rent increases and must specify the current rent, new rent, start date, and calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Email delivery is permitted only if the renter has consented to receiving notices by email. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, **if the agent only sent an ordinary email and did not give you a completed prescribed notice, the rent increase is not valid**. You do not have to pay the higher rent on the basis of that email. A rent increase that contravenes these requirements is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not specify a payable date for your particular increase because no valid notice date is provided. If a valid notice is later given, the increase could take effect **no earlier than 60 days after that notice is given**, subject to the other statutory requirements. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Continue paying the existing rent while there is no valid rent-increase notice.  
- Ask the agent to provide the completed **Form 5**, including the calculation method and proposed start date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019**—the version in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- A landlord had to maintain the rented premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- For **non-urgent repairs**, after giving written notice, you could apply to the Director for an investigation if the repairs were not completed within 14 days; after the Director’s report, you could apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A **month-to-month agreement is a periodic agreement**. For a notice to vacate **without specifying a reason**, the notice generally had to give at least **120 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A notice under the no-reason provision had **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- Any notice to vacate had to be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason if one was relied on, and state the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- If the notice claimed the landlord needed to carry out repairs, the landlord had to show that the work required you to vacate, that necessary permits and consents had been obtained, and give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should check and do

1. **Check the notice’s stated ground.** If it says “no reason,” check whether the termination date is at least **120 days after the notice date** and whether the notice was issued because you exercised a repair-related right. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 1 October 2025 (*Residential Tenancies Act 1997* v110 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* v004 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)):

### What the law says about the situation

**Advertising the property with photos showing mould**
The legislation does not explicitly forbid a rental provider from including photos that show mould in a rental advertisement. Under section 89A of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a provider is permitted to enter the premises to produce advertising images after providing the required notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

**Minimum standards and mould**
Under Schedule 4 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, the rental minimum standard for mould states: *"Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Section 65A of the Act further requires that a provider ensure the premises comply with these standards on or before the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

Regarding whether a photo is enough to prove non-compliance: The retrieved documents do not specify evidentiary rules for photographs. However, because the legal standard specifically hinges on the **cause** of the mould (i.e., whether it stems from a structural defect rather than condensation from daily living), a photograph alone generally does not establish a breach. Proving non-compliance would typically require evidence linking the mould to the building's structure.

### What you can do or ask

**Regarding the advertisement:**
* **Object in writing:** If the photo shows your possessions that identify you, reveal sensitive information, are valuable, or might identify someone at risk of family violence, send a written objection to the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Request a review & withhold consent:** You can ask to review the images before they are advertised. The provider must not publish them until you have reviewed them and given written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Regarding the mould:**
* **Request a formal inspection:** Ask the provider to inspect the property to determine the cause of the mould. 
* **Raise a minimum standards breach:** If the mould is structural, request that it be treated as a failure to meet the rental minimum standards under section 65A of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Request urgent repairs:** If the premises do not comply with the standards upon or immediately after you move in, you may issue a formal request for urgent repairs to bring the property into compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on **1 October 2025**, here is the relevant information from the retrieved documents:

### 📜 Applicable Law & Documents
*   ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Vic), version 110 (Authorised Version in force from 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
*   ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, version 004 (Authorised Version in force from 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### ⚖️ What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a landlord is legally entitled to give you a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice must specify a termination date that is at least **60 days** after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

**Crucially, the retrieved documents do not state that a notice to vacate automatically becomes invalid or lapses if the buyer pulls out or the sale falls through.** Once validly issued, the notice remains in force until the stated termination date unless it is formally withdrawn by the landlord or set aside by VCAT.

### 🛡️ What You Can Do
*   **Do not leave immediately just because the sale fell through:** The notice remains legally active until the termination date. However, you are not required to vacate before that date simply because the buyer withdrew [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
*   **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If you believe the notice was not given properly, the information on it is incorrect or incomplete, or the reason given is invalid, you may be able to challenge it at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Attend any VCAT hearing:** If your landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order because you haven't left by the termination date, you are strongly encouraged to attend the hearing. VCAT will decide if you must leave and on what date. You can ask for more time if leaving would cause you hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
*   **Request a voluntary withdrawal:** While the provided excerpts do not detail a statutory withdrawal process for standard tenancies, you can ask your landlord to voluntarily withdraw the notice in writing. If they agree, they should formally cancel the eviction process [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### 🚫 Important Eviction Rules
Even if the notice remains valid and the termination date passes, **your landlord cannot personally use force to remove you**. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT possession order (a warrant for possession) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

*Note: If you are unsure about your specific grounds for challenging the notice or how to prepare for a VCAT hearing, you should seek immediate advice from a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).*

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 1 March 2023, here is the relevant information:

### What the law says about electrical circuits
There is **no rule in Victorian tenancy law that specifies a minimum number of electrical circuits** a rental property must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The legislation does not dictate how power points or appliances should be grouped onto circuits. 

However, under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 002), a new electrical safety standard is scheduled to take effect on **29 March 2023** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). From that date, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can ask for and do
While the law does not mandate a specific circuit count, your rental provider has a legal duty under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997, version 101) to maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A breaker that trips when running standard appliances indicates an electrical fault or overload that requires professional assessment. You can take the following steps:

1. **Request an electrical safety check record:** You can ask your rental provider for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check. They are legally required to provide this within 7 days of receiving your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Report the issue in writing:** Notify your rental provider in writing about the tripping breaker and the breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
   * If the power outage affects an essential service (such as heating or cooking), it may be classified as an **urgent repair**, which the provider must fix immediately after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   * If it is considered a **non-urgent repair**, the provider must carry it out within a reasonable time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Escalate to VCAT if ignored:** If the rental provider does not address the issue within a reasonable time (typically 14 days for non-urgent repairs), you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

*Note: The new circuit breaker and RCD safety standard will take effect in just over a month (29 March 2023). If your current switchboard lacks these compliant safety devices, you can flag this when requesting your electrical safety check record.*

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Version 088** (which was in force on 1 November 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here is what you should check if you believe your notice to vacate is retaliatory:

### 1. Whether the Notice is Invalid Due to Retaliation
The Act explicitly protects renters from eviction notices that are given in response to them exercising their legal rights. Parallel provisions for other tenancy types confirm that a notice to vacate is **of no effect** if it was given in response to the exercise (or proposed exercise) of a right under the Act, such as requesting repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Your tenancy agreement also falls under section 91ZM, which governs notices to vacate for standard residential tenancies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You should verify that your notice does not violate this anti-retaliation protection.

### 2. The Stated Reason and Minimum Notice Period
Check the reason listed on the notice against the statutory minimum notice periods required by the Act. For example:
*   A notice for **non-payment of rent** must specify a termination date of at least **14 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
*   A notice for **use of premises for an illegal purpose** must also specify a termination date of at least **14 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
If the reason listed does not match the actual grounds, or if the termination date falls short of the legally required timeframe for that specific reason, the notice may be invalid.

### 3. The Strict Deadline to Challenge the Notice
You must act quickly. The Act imposes strict time limits on challenging a notice to vacate. You are **not entitled** to apply to the Tribunal to challenge the validity of a notice after the end of **14 days** from the date it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you miss this window, you lose your statutory right to contest its validity through the Tribunal.

### What You Can Do
*   **Document everything:** Keep copies of your repair requests and the exact date you received the notice to establish a timeline showing the connection between your request and the eviction.
*   **Apply to the Tribunal promptly:** If you believe the notice is retaliatory or invalid, file an application with the Tribunal within the 14-day deadline to have its validity challenged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
*   **Do not ignore the notice:** Even if you plan to challenge it, continue to pay rent and comply with your tenancy obligations until the Tribunal makes a determination or the termination date passes.

*Note: This guidance is based strictly on the provided excerpts from Version 088 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic) effective in November 2019.*

### What the law says
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115, in force on 13 October 2026), a residential rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to you keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The law sets a strict deadline for handling these requests: if the provider does not apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within **14 days** after receiving your request, they are legally **taken to have consented** to you keeping the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Can they refuse based on the owner's allergy?
The agent cannot simply say "no" and stop there. While an owner's health condition or allergy can be a factor in determining whether a refusal is "reasonable," the provider must actively prove this reason to the Tribunal within that 14-day window [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Because three weeks have passed and the agent only verbally/written refused without applying to VCAT, they are deemed to have given consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The fact that the owner hardly ever visits does not automatically make the refusal reasonable; if a dispute were to go to court, the Tribunal would weigh all relevant circumstances (such as the type of pet, the nature of the premises, and the frequency of the owner's visits) to decide if refusing consent was justified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Notify the agent in writing:** Inform the agent that because more than 14 days have passed since you submitted your official request form, consent has been legally deemed given under section 71C(2) of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Keep the pet:** You are now legally permitted to keep the dog on the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they threaten eviction or removal:** The agent cannot issue a valid notice to vacate or force you to remove the pet unless they first obtain a Tribunal order excluding the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they attempt to do so without one, it would be unlawful.

### What the law says about fixing damage secretly
The law requires you to be transparent about any damage caused by you or your pet. Under section 61, you must not negligently cause damage to the rented premises (which does not include fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If damage occurs, section 62 mandates that you must give written notice to your landlord as soon as practicable, detailing both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

You **cannot** simply fix it without telling the owner. Failing to report it breaches your statutory duty to notify [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, under sections 78 and 79, your landlord has the right to issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days (in a tradesman-like manner), or they can choose to repair it themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Hiding the damage could lead to disputes over the quality of the repair or the cost, especially since the initial condition report is used to verify responsibility for damage at the end of your tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Notify your landlord immediately:** Send written notice (email is acceptable under the Electronic Transactions Act) detailing that your dog chewed the skirting boards and describing the extent of the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Propose a solution:** Ask your landlord if they would prefer to hire a tradesperson or if they allow you to arrange the repair yourself. If they agree to let you fix it, ensure you get written confirmation and keep all receipts.
3. **Agree on costs:** Be prepared to pay for the repairs.
